description: We are No Risk No Fun: six Cairo students turning mission design into something you can play. We build fast, interfaces, simulation, data, and cinematic visuals, and our SpaceX simulator already shows how every payload choice moves mass, power, data, and budget. Join us if you can model orbital mechanics, design clear interfaces, or make hard ideas simple; we are looking for systems thinkers, frontend builders, and science communicators who want to ship a working mission loop in 48 hours.
summary:
SpaceX is a browser-based space mission design game built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. A player picks one of three missions — POLAR WATCH at Earth, LUNAR ICE at the Moon, MARS DUST at Mars — reads the science brief, assembles a spacecraft on a live 3D bench, flies the mission, and gets a scored report explaining exactly why it worked or failed. Five stages, no reloads: mission select, brief, design, flight, report.

It addresses the challenge by making real mission trade-offs playable instead of abstract. Every part choice feeds a deterministic model of mass, power, downlink, radiation and cost against the mission's budget and launch capacity, and Fly only unlocks when the design can actually do the job. The 3D spacecraft, the resource meters and the flight scene all read one shared assembly model, so what you build is what you fly. NASA Earth and planetary imagery is shipped with the site and credited in-app.

It matters because it turns NASA data and engineering constraints into something a student, a classroom or a team can experience in minutes — and multiplayer party mode lets a whole room design and fly the same mission together.
details:
**SpaceX** is a browser-based space mission design game. A player chooses one of three missions — POLAR WATCH (Earth), LUNAR ICE (Moon), MARS DUST (Mars) — reads the science brief, builds a spacecraft on a live 3D bench, flies the mission, and receives a scored report explaining why it worked or failed. Five stages run without reloads: mission select, brief, design, flight, report.

It works as a single deterministic model. The bench asks five questions — spacecraft, power, payload, orbit and lifetime, flight configuration — and every choice feeds the same evaluator, checking mass, power margin, downlink, radiation and cost against the mission's budget and launch capacity. **Fly** unlocks only when the design can genuinely do the job. The 3D hull, the resource meters and the flight scene all read one shared assembly model, so the craft you build is the craft you fly. Flight plays as one continuous shot: launch, ascent, orbit insertion, operations, then a 0–100 report.

The benefit is that mission engineering becomes something a student or a classroom can attempt in minutes: the constraints are real, the feedback is immediate, and failure is explanatory rather than a wall. Multiplayer party mode extends this — one room code and a team designs, flies and reads the same report together.

Built with Preact 11, strict TypeScript, Vite 6, three.js with hand-written GLSL, three isolated 3D renderers, Vitest, and Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects. Creativity came from making the design bench, the brief and the flight one spacecraft instead of three illustrations, and from the shared-session party mode. We prioritised offline reliability, honest educational data, accessibility, and never showing a blank frame between stages.
